title: snarktank/ralph
abstract:
Ralph Ralph is an autonomous AI agent loop that runs AI coding tools ( Amp or Claude Code ) repeatedly until all PRD items are complete. Each iteration is a fresh instance with clean context. Memory persists via git history, progress.txt , and prd.json . Based on Geoffrey Huntley's Ralph pattern . Read my in-depth article on how I use Ralph Prerequisites One of the following AI coding tools installed and authenticated: Amp CLI (default) Claude Code ( npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code ) jq installed ( brew install jq on macOS) A git repository for your project Setup Option 1: Copy to your project Copy the ralph files into your project: # From your project root mkdir -p scripts/ralph
cp /path/to/ralph/ralph.sh scripts/ralph/ # Copy the prompt template for your AI tool of choice: cp /path/to/ralph/prompt.md scripts/ralph/prompt.md # For Amp # OR cp /path/to/ralph/CLAUDE.md scripts/ralph/CLAUDE.md # For Claude Code chmod +x scripts/ralph/ralph.sh Option 2: Install skills globally (Amp) Copy the skills to your Amp or Claude config for use across all projects: For AMP cp -r skills/prd ~ /.config/amp/skills/
cp -r skills/ralph ~ /.config/amp/skills/ For Claude Code (manual) cp -r skills/prd ~ /.claude/skills/
cp -r skills/ralph ~ /.claude/skills/ Option 3: Use as Claude Code Marketplace Add the Ralph marketplace to Claude Code: /plugin marketplace add snarktank/ralph Then install the skills: /plugin install ralph-skills@ralph-marketplace Available skills after installation: /prd - Generate Product Requirements Documents /ralph - Convert PRDs to prd.json format Skills are automatically invoked when you ask Claude to: "create a prd", "write prd for", "plan this feature" "convert this prd", "turn into ralph format", "create prd.json" Configure Amp auto-handoff (recommended) Add to ~/.config/amp/settings.json : { "amp.experimental.autoHandoff" : { "context" : 90 }
} This enables automatic handoff when context fills up, allowing Ralph to handle large stories that exceed a single context window. Workflow 1. Create a PRD Use the PRD skill to generate a detailed requirements document: Load the prd skill and create a PRD for [your feature description] Answer the clarifying questions. The skill saves output to tasks/prd-[feature-name].md . 2. Convert PRD to Ralph format Use the Ralph skill to convert the markdown PRD to JSON: Load the ralph skill and convert tasks/prd-[feature-name].md to prd.json This creates prd.json with user stories structured for autonomous execution. 3. Run Ralph # Using Amp (default) ./scripts/ralph/ralph.sh [max_iterations] # Using Claude Code ./scripts/ralph/ralph.sh --tool claude [max_iterations] Default is 10 iterations. Use --tool amp or --tool claude to select your AI coding tool. Ralph will: Create a feature branch (from PRD branchName ) Pick the highest priority story where passes: false Implement that single story Run quality checks (typecheck, tests) Commit if checks pass Update prd.json to mark story as passes: true Append learnings to progress.txt Repeat until all stories pass or max iterations reached Key Files File Purpose ralph.sh The bash loop that spawns fresh AI instances (supports --tool amp or --tool claude ) prompt.md Prompt template for Amp CLAUDE.md Prompt template for Claude Code prd.json User stories with passes status (the task list) prd.json.example Example PRD format for reference progress.txt Append-only learnings for future iterations skills/prd/ Skill for generating PRDs (works with Amp and Claude Code) skills/ralph/ Skill for converting PRDs to JSON (works with Amp and Claude Code) .claude-plugin/ Plugin manifest for Claude Code marketplace discovery flowchart/ Interactive visualization of how Ralph works Flowchart View Interactive Flowchart - Click through to see each step with animations. The flowchart/ directory contains the source code. To run locally: cd flowchart
npm install
npm run dev Critical Concepts Each Iteration = Fresh Context Each iteration spawns a new AI instance (Amp or Claude Code) with clean context. The only memory between iterations is: Git history (commits from previous iterations) progress.txt (learnings and context) prd.json (which stories are done) Small Tasks Each PRD item should be small enough to complete in one context window. If a task is too big, the LLM runs out of context before finishing and produces poor code. Right-sized stories: Add a database column and migration Add a UI component to an existing page Update a server action with new logic Add a filter dropdown to a list Too big (split these): "Build the entire dashboard" "Add authentication" "Refactor the API" AGENTS.md Updates Are Critical After each iteration, Ralph updates the relevant AGENTS.md files with learnings. This is key because AI coding tools automatically read these files, so future iterations (and future human developers) benefit from discovered patterns, gotchas, and conventions. Examples of what to add to AGENTS.md: Patterns discovered ("this codebase uses X for Y") Gotchas ("do not forget to update Z when changing W") Useful context ("the settings panel is in component X") Feedback Loops Ralph only works if there are feedback loops: Typecheck catches type errors Tests verify behavior CI must stay green (broken code compounds across iterations) Browser Verification for UI Stories Frontend stories must include "Verify in browser using dev-browser skill" in acceptance criteria. Ralph will use the dev-browser skill to navigate to the page, interact with the UI, and confirm changes work. Stop Condition When all stories have passes: true , Ralph outputs <promise>COMPLETE</promise> and the loop exits. Debugging Check current state: # See which stories are done cat prd.json | jq ' .userStories[] | {id, title, passes} ' # See learnings from previous iterations cat progress.txt # Check git history git log --oneline -10 Customizing the Prompt After copying prompt.md (for Amp) or CLAUDE.md (for Claude Code) to your project, customize it for your project: Add project-specific quality check commands Include codebase conventions Add common gotchas for your stack Archiving Ralph automatically archives previous runs when you start a new feature (different branchName ). Archives are saved to archive/YYYY-MM-DD-feature-name/ . References Geoffrey Huntley's Ralph article Amp documentation Claude Code documentation

title: poco-ai/Agentero
abstract:
為人與 Agent 協作而生的一站式科研工作臺 保留人類舒適的 PDF 閱讀習慣，為模型提供純淨的結構化上下文；文獻、筆記與互動記錄統一沉澱於本地。 中文 | English 如果本專案對你有幫助，請在右上角 給個 star 吧！ 背景與設計初衷 Zotero 是學術管理領域非常優秀的軟體。它功能成熟、生態穩定，幫助許多科研人員建立了最初的文獻歸檔體系。 但在當下日常科研與深度使用各類 Agent 時，傳統的文獻工具鏈暴露出一些斷點： 上下文嚴重分散 ：論文儲存在 Zotero，筆記記在 Obsidian，與模型的推導和分析留在各個網頁對話方塊中。三者資料彼此隔離，當需要 Agent 結合某篇具體論文與歷史筆記進行深入推導時，使用者必須反覆手動複製貼上。 文獻格式對模型不友好 ：人類習慣閱讀排版良好的 PDF 檔案；但對於模型而言，直接解析雙欄排版、跨頁表格、複雜數學公式和交叉引用的成本極高，極易產生識別錯誤與幻覺。結構化 Markdown 與 LaTeX 才是模型容易準確理解的格式。 維護成本較高 ：AI 伴讀、全文翻譯、筆記同步等高頻需求，往往需要安裝和除錯多個社群外掛，配置門檻高且在版本升級時容易出現相容性問題。 批次自動化能力有限 ：通過 Deep Research 或自動化檢索工具發現的大量文獻，目前仍需人工在瀏覽器中逐篇點選儲存，難以順暢銜接批次研究流。 Agentero 並非旨在替代 Zotero，而是探索一種人與 Agent 協同處理科研上下文的新方式 ： 人類負責 ：提出研究問題、進行學術價值判斷、深度研讀與核心結論推導； Agent 負責 ：批次檢索篩選、後設資料抓取、圖表與公式提取、引用關係梳理及基礎總結。 核心功能 1. 結構化閱讀與筆記系統 PDF 閱讀與批註 ：提供大綱導航、整頁與寬度自適應、平滑劃詞、高亮批註與全文檢索。 圖表與公式提取 ：自動解析論文中的數學公式、演算法虛擬碼及表格，生成結構化 Markdown 與 LaTeX 內容，確保 Agent 呼叫時上下文準確無誤。 雙向連結筆記 ：內建所見即所得 Markdown 編輯器，支援 [[雙鏈]] 引用語法、 / 快捷指令與 LaTeX 即時渲染，筆記與文獻建立原生關聯。 多模式翻譯服務 ：支援劃詞翻譯、按頁對照翻譯與全文翻譯，內建可用翻譯通道，並支援配置自定義 API Key（BYOK）。 分屏閱讀與分析：左側高亮批註，右側本地 Agent 基於準確的結構化上下文進行答疑與推導 劃詞翻譯與即時記錄：閱讀過程中提取的要點可直接沉澱至本地 Markdown 筆記 2. 開放的 Agent 協議與自動化介面 基於 ACP 協議連線本地 Agent ：底層遵循 Agent Client Protocol，支援連線各類本地執行的 Agent（如 Claude Code、OpenCode、Codex 或本地模型），不綁定特定廠商，上下文完全保留在本地。 內建 MCP (Model Context Protocol) ：可作為 MCP Server 執行，允許 ChatGPT Web、Claude Desktop 等外部客戶端直接檢索並呼叫本地文獻庫作為上下文。 極客 CLI 支援 ：內建無頭命令列工具，支援通過指令碼實現批次匯入文獻、提取後設資料與寫入筆記等自動化工作流。 內建 MCP 協議服務，支援將本地文獻庫無縫接入各類外部 AI 客戶端 3. 學術雷達與文獻發現 多渠道抓取 ：內建整合 Cool Papers 與魔搭社群，支援在軟體內直接瀏覽並一鍵歸檔文獻；支援學術 RSS 訂閱。 個性化推薦 ：基於本地已有文獻庫的內容特徵，自動推薦每日 arXiv 的相關最新論文。 引用關係自動梳理 ：自動解析文獻末尾的參考文獻列表，支援一鍵批次抓取入庫；支援獲取出版商後設資料並追蹤後續被引動態。 應用內直接瀏覽 Cool Papers 熱門論文並一鍵匯入本地知識庫 4. 相容 Zotero 生態與本地透明儲存 Zotero 書庫無縫遷移 ：支援一鍵匯入整個 Zotero 資料庫，保留已有標籤、筆記與附件；相容 Zotero 瀏覽器擴展直接儲存網頁論文；支援匯出 BibTeX / BibLaTeX。 本地資料夾透明管理 ：不使用私有資料庫或雜湊混淆目錄，所有文獻與筆記均以標準檔案（PDF、Markdown）儲存在本地規範檔案夾中，可自由使用外部編輯器讀取。 多端同步與遠端訪問 ：支援與 S3 相容的雲端儲存服務進行同步；支援通過 SSH 隧道訪問部署在遠端伺服器上的文獻庫。 介面與功能預覽 點選展開：檢視更多介面截圖（RSS 訂閱、技能擴展、Agent 配置、S3 雲同步、主題風格） 1. 學術 RSS 訂閱 追蹤關注的學術部落格、實驗室主頁與前沿動態： 2. Agent 技能（Skill）擴展 瀏覽並安裝社群提供的科研技能，擴展論文精讀與寫作分析能力： 3. Agent 與連線配置 通過 ACP 協議管理、升級和切換本地 Agent： 4. S3 相容雲端儲存同步 配置私有或商業 S3 儲存，實現多裝置間知識庫同步： 5. 多套介面主題 支援亮色/暗色及多種配色風格，支援自適應系統外觀設定： 快速開始 桌面客戶端安裝 (macOS / Windows / Linux) 可前往 官網 agentero.app 或 GitHub Releases 下載適用於各平臺的預編譯安裝包。 macOS (Homebrew) brew tap poco-ai/agentero
brew install --cask agentero Linux 使用者須知 ：系統環境要求 Ubuntu 22.04+（依賴 webkit2gtk 4.1 ），詳細依賴說明請參考 安裝文件 。 命令列工具 (CLI) 如需在終端或通過指令碼自動化管理文獻： brew tap poco-ai/agentero
brew install agentero # 檢視常用命令與參數 agentero --help 在更多地方使用 Agentero DeepSeek Harness (dsh) 外掛 ：在 DeepSeek Harness 中也能直接使用 Agentero 的文獻庫、筆記與 PDF 閱讀器。執行 dsh plugin --profile web add @poco-ai/agentero-dsh 安裝，詳見 agentero-dsh-plugin 。 致謝與社群 感謝 LinuxDo 與 ModelScope 魔搭社群 成員在專案早期測試階段提供的建議與反饋。 感謝 AtomGit 提供的國內映象支援。 使用者交流群 掃碼加入微信群：使用心得、問題反饋與版本預告。二維碼 7 天內有效，過期請在 Issue 留言。 如果 Agentero 對你的日常學術研究有所幫助，歡迎在 GitHub 上為本專案點亮一個 ⭐ Star 。 感謝所有貢獻者！ Star History 開源許可證 本專案基於 MIT License 協議開源。第三方元件與許可證清單見 .github/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md 。

title: Open-Dev-Society/OpenStock
abstract:
SPONSORED BY Orbit . Free, open-source macOS screen recorder, screenshot tool and video editor: auto-zoom, smooth cursor, backgrounds, web recordings and AI agent recording. Open OpenStock · Changelog · Self-host it · Sponsor · Discord OpenStock Markets, minus the paywall. OpenStock is a free, open-source alternative to expensive market platforms: track prices, watch the whole market and dig into company insights. Use it at openstock-ods.vercel.app , or run your own copy with every feature. ❤️ 13,000+ people use OpenStock for free. Help keep it that way: sponsor from $5 a month , or read how OpenStock is funded . Note OpenStock is community-built and not a brokerage. Market data may be delayed depending on the provider and your setup. Nothing here is financial advice. 📋 Table of Contents 🔋 Features ⏱️ How fresh is the data ⚙️ Tech stack 🤸 Quick start 🔐 Environment variables 🐳 Self-hosting : Docker, prebuilt image, one-click deploys, Vercel 🧱 Project structure 📡 How it works 🌍 Market support 🧪 Scripts and tests 🤝 Contributing 🏆 Contributors 🛡️ Security 📜 License 🌱 Open Dev Society manifesto 🙏 Acknowledgements ❤️ Sponsor OpenStock 🔋 Features Markets A dashboard for eight markets: US, India, Germany, Canada, Australia, Saudi Arabia, Crypto and Forex, with an index pulse, a sector heatmap, market leaders and top stories. Search every exchange Finnhub covers with ⌘K , and keep stocks open as browser-style tabs. Stock pages TradingView candles with drawing tools (trend lines, Fibonacci, shapes, text) and fullscreen. Pick indicators once (SMA, EMA, Bollinger Bands, VWAP, RSI, MACD, Stochastic, ATR) and they stay on every chart. Financials, technicals and the company profile. Sentiment from Reddit, X, news and Polymarket (with an Adanos key). Watchlist and alerts A watchlist of up to 50 stocks, saved to your account. Price alerts above or below a target, checked every 5 minutes and emailed to you (in realtime mode). A weekly, AI-written news digest by email every Monday. Accounts Email and password, plus Google and GitHub sign-in when configured; password reset and a profile page. Rate-limited sign-in, sign-up and password reset; resetting your password signs out your other devices. Community A changelog that credits everyone who contributed, a Wall of love , and an update banner in the app. ⏱️ How fresh is the data Charts always stream live from TradingView. Quotes, watchlist prices and alerts come from Finnhub: Quotes Price alerts Cost Community : openstock-ods.vercel.app Every hour, shared by everyone No Free OpenStock Cloud (coming soon) Every 15 seconds By email $5 a month Self-hosted Every hour, or every 15 seconds with NEXT_PUBLIC_OPENSTOCK_DATA_MODE=realtime and your own Finnhub keys By email, in realtime mode Free ⚙️ Tech stack App Next.js 15 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, shadcn/ui and Radix Accounts and data Better Auth, MongoDB with Mongoose Market data Finnhub, TradingView widgets, Adanos (sentiment) Background jobs Inngest Email Nodemailer (Gmail), Kit for the newsletter AI Gemini, MiniMax or Siray Hosting Vercel; a Docker image on GitHub Container Registry for self-hosting 🤸 Quick start You need Node.js 22 LTS, a MongoDB database (a free Atlas cluster, or the Docker setup ) and a free Finnhub key. git clone https://github.com/Open-Dev-Society/OpenStock.git cd OpenStock
npm ci
cp .env.example .env # fill in MONGODB_URI, BETTER_AUTH_SECRET and FINNHUB_API_KEY node scripts/check-env.mjs # checks your .env npm run test:db # checks the MongoDB connection npm run dev # http://localhost:3000 Welcome emails, price alerts and the weekly digest run as Inngest jobs. Locally, start Inngest's dev server alongside the app: npx inngest-cli@latest dev . For production: npm run build && npm start . 🔐 Environment variables Every variable is listed with comments in .env.example . The ones that matter: Variable Needed What it's for MONGODB_URI Yes Your MongoDB database BETTER_AUTH_SECRET Yes Signs sessions. Generate it with openssl rand -hex 32 . Auth refuses to run in production without it BETTER_AUTH_URL Yes The app's public URL, used for auth callbacks and links in emails FINNHUB_API_KEY Yes Market data. Or put several free keys, comma-separated, in FINNHUB_API_KEYS : they're rotated, and each adds 60 requests a minute NEXT_PUBLIC_OPENSTOCK_DATA_MODE No cached (hourly, the default) or realtime (every 15 seconds, with price alerts). Fixed when the app is built: rebuild after changing it INNGEST_SIGNING_KEY , INNGEST_EVENT_KEY In production Background jobs: welcome emails, price alerts and the weekly digest NODEMAILER_EMAIL , NODEMAILER_PASSWORD No Sending email through Gmail, with an app password. Without them, emails are skipped GEMINI_API_KEY (or MiniMax or Siray) No AI-written welcome emails and the news digest ADANOS_API_KEY No The sentiment card on stock pages KIT_API_KEY , KIT_API_SECRET , KIT_WELCOME_FORM_ID No The weekly digest newsletter in Kit GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID / _SECRET , GITHUB_CLIENT_ID / _SECRET No Social sign-in. Callbacks: <BETTER_AUTH_URL>/api/auth/callback/google and /github NEXT_PUBLIC_FINNHUB_API_KEY still works as a name for the Finnhub key. No key is ever sent to the browser. 🐳 Self-hosting Docker Compose Runs OpenStock and MongoDB together. MongoDB is only reachable inside the Docker network; it isn't published on your machine. Fill in .env (see above). For the bundled database, choose a password and use it in both places. Letters and digits are simplest; @ : / ? # must be percent-encoded in the URI. MONGO_ROOT_PASSWORD = change-me MONGODB_URI = mongodb://root:change-me@mongodb:27017/openstock?authSource=admin Start it: docker compose up -d --build Open http://localhost:3000 The image build needs no secrets: every variable is read when the container starts, except NEXT_PUBLIC_OPENSTOCK_DATA_MODE , which Compose passes to the build from .env . Data lives in the mongo-data volume, and the MongoDB password is only applied when that volume is first created. Prebuilt image Every push to main publishes ghcr.io/open-dev-society/openstock for amd64 and arm64, tagged latest , sha-<commit> , and a version for each release (for example 2026.10.18 ). To use it, replace build: under openstock in docker-compose.yml with: image : ghcr.io/open-dev-society/openstock:latest then run docker compose pull && docker compose up -d . The prebuilt image runs in cached mode; build it yourself for realtime. One-click deploys Railway OpenStock ships a railway.json that builds the Dockerfile , checks health on /sign-in and restarts on failure. The template above sets everything up; to do it by hand: Create a project and add a MongoDB database ( + New → Database → MongoDB ). Add a service from this repository ( + New → GitHub Repo ). In the service's Variables , set: MONGODB_URI = ${ {MongoDB.MONGO_URL } } BETTER_AUTH_SECRET = ${ {secret(32) } } BETTER_AUTH_URL = https:// ${ {RAILWAY_PUBLIC_DOMAIN } } FINNHUB_API_KEY = your_finnhub_key GEMINI_API_KEY = your_gemini_api_key INNGEST_SIGNING_KEY = your_inngest_signing_key INNGEST_EVENT_KEY = your_inngest_event_key NODEMAILER_EMAIL = youraddress@gmail.com NODEMAILER_PASSWORD = your_gmail_app_password Under Settings → Networking , generate a public domain and redeploy. For background jobs, add your Railway domain as an app in the Inngest dashboard , pointing to https://<your-domain>/api/inngest . To turn on realtime mode, also set NEXT_PUBLIC_OPENSTOCK_DATA_MODE=realtime ; Railway passes it to the build. Vercel Import the repository, set the variables above for Production, and connect Inngest (its Vercel integration sets both keys). vercel.json pins functions to Mumbai ( bom1 ), next to the hosted database; change it to the region nearest yours.

更推薦使用「整個元素」的動畫，而不是把文字拆成很多碎片逐字亂動。這樣畫面更穩、可讀性更好，也更適合匯出和二次編輯。動畫主要用於引導視線和表達層級，不建議做複雜時間線、高頻閃爍、無限迴圈或大幅抖動。 🦙 支援本地 Ollama 模型（OpenAI 相容） 專案支援通過 OpenAI 相容協議 接入本地 Ollama。 在「設定」頁面這樣填寫即可： provider : openai base_url 官方端點不會攜帶非標準的 thinking 參數，避免返回 400 Unknown parameter ；配置其他 OpenAI 相容 base_url 時仍會請求關閉 thinking，避免工具呼叫等多輪鏈路丟失 reasoning_content 。 Ollama 配置用於文本生成、文件解析和編輯對話；需要生圖或自動配圖時，請在「設定 → 生圖模型」另行配置支援圖片生成的 Provider。 配置並點選「驗證」。驗證會實際生成一張測試圖片；驗證成功後才能儲存該生圖模型，隨後即可在建立頁和編輯頁中選擇使用。 關於預覽模式 支援鍵盤左右鍵切換頁面；支援演示模式和全屏演示模式，按 ESC 退出演示。 關於匯出 目前支援五種匯出方式，另可將 HTML 演示稿打包為獨立開啟的檔案： PDF ：適合直接分享、歸檔和列印。 PNG ：一鍵批次匯出所有頁面圖片，適合插入文件、Notion、公眾號或社媒內容。 PNG 長圖 ：將整套頁面縱向拼接成一張長圖，適合發社媒、聊天分享、長文件預覽和移動端閱讀。 可編輯 PPTX ：純自研匯出底層，常規場景還原度接近 100%，可在 PowerPoint / Keynote 中繼續編輯。 MP4 ：匯出為影片檔案，適合釋出到社媒、傳送給客戶或在不方便播放 PPT 的場景中使用。 HTML title: humanlayer/12-factor-agents
abstract: 12-Factor Agents - Principles for building reliable LLM applications In the spirit of 12 Factor Apps . The source for this project is public at https://github.com/humanlayer/12-factor-agents , and I welcome your feedback and contributions. Let's figure this out together! Tip Missed the AI Engineer World's Fair? Catch the talk here Looking for Context Engineering? Jump straight to factor 3 Want to contribute to npx/uvx create-12-factor-agent - check out the discussion thread Hi, I'm Dex. I've been hacking on AI agents for a while . I've tried every agent framework out there , from the plug-and-play crew/langchains to the "minimalist" smolagents of the world to the "production grade" langraph, griptape, etc. I've talked to a lot of really strong founders , in and out of YC, who are all building really impressive things with AI. Most of them are rolling the stack themselves. I don't see a lot of frameworks in production customer-facing agents. I've been surprised to find that most of the products out there billing themselves as "AI Agents" are not all that agentic. A lot of them are mostly deterministic code, with LLM steps sprinkled in at just the right points to make the experience truly magical. Agents, at least the good ones, don't follow the "here's your prompt, here's a bag of tools, loop until you hit the goal" pattern. Rather, they are comprised of mostly just software. So, I set out to answer: What are the principles we can use to build LLM-powered software that is actually good enough to put in the hands of production customers? Welcome to 12-factor agents. As every Chicago mayor since Daley has consistently plastered all over the city's major airports, we're glad you're here. Special thanks to @iantbutler01 , @tnm , @hellovai , @stantonk , @balanceiskey , @AdjectiveAllison , @pfbyjy , @a-churchill , and the SF MLOps community for early feedback on this guide. The Short Version: The 12 Factors Even if LLMs continue to get exponentially more powerful , there will be core engineering techniques that make LLM-powered software more reliable, more scalable, and easier to maintain. How We Got Here: A Brief History of Software Factor 1: Natural Language to Tool Calls Factor 2: Own your prompts Factor 3: Own your context window Factor 4: Tools are just structured outputs Factor 5: Unify execution state and business state Factor 6: Launch/Pause/Resume with simple APIs Factor 7: Contact humans with tool calls Factor 8: Own your control flow Factor 9: Compact Errors into Context Window Factor 10: Small, Focused Agents Factor 11: Trigger from anywhere, meet users where they are Factor 12: Make your agent a stateless reducer Visual Nav How we got here For a deeper dive on my agent journey and what led us here, check out A Brief History of Software - a quick summary here: The promise of agents We're gonna talk a lot about Directed Graphs (DGs) and their Acyclic friends, DAGs. I'll start by pointing out that...well...software is a directed graph. There's a reason we used to represent programs as flow charts. From code to DAGs Around 20 years ago, we started to see DAG orchestrators become popular. We're talking classics like Airflow , Prefect , some predecessors, and some newer ones like ( dagster , inggest , windmill ). These followed the same graph pattern, with the added benefit of observability, modularity, retries, administration, etc. The promise of agents I'm not the first person to say this , but my biggest takeaway when I started learning about agents, was that you get to throw the DAG away. Instead of software engineers coding each step and edge case, you can give the agent a goal and a set of transitions: And let the LLM make decisions in real time to figure out the path The promise here is that you write less software, you just give the LLM the "edges" of the graph and let it figure out the nodes. You can recover from errors, you can write less code, and you may find that LLMs find novel solutions to problems. Agents as loops As we'll see later, it turns out this doesn't quite work. Let's dive one step deeper - with agents you've got this loop consisting of 3 steps: LLM determines the next step in the workflow, outputting structured json ("tool calling") Deterministic code executes the tool call The result is appended to the context window Repeat until the next step is determined to be "done" initial_event = { "message" : "..." } context = [ initial_event ] while True : next_step = await llm . determine_next_step ( context ) context . append ( next_step ) if ( next_step . intent == = "done" ): return next_step . final_answer result = await execute_step ( next_step ) context . append ( result ) Our initial context is just the starting event (maybe a user message, maybe a cron fired, maybe a webhook, etc), and we ask the llm to choose the next step (tool) or to determine that we're done. Here's a multi-step example: 027-agent-loop-animation.mp4 GIF Version Why 12-factor agents? At the end of the day, this approach just doesn't work as well as we want it to. In building HumanLayer, I've talked to at least 100 SaaS builders (mostly technical founders) looking to make their existing product more agentic. The journey usually goes something like: Decide you want to build an agent Product design, UX mapping, what problems to solve Want to move fast, so grab $FRAMEWORK and get to building Get to 70-80% quality bar Realize that 80% isn't good enough for most customer-facing features Realize that getting past 80% requires reverse-engineering the framework, prompts, flow, etc. Start over from scratch Random Disclaimers DISCLAIMER : I'm not sure the exact right place to say this, but here seems as good as any: this in BY NO MEANS meant to be a dig on either the many frameworks out there, or the pretty dang smart people who work on them . They enable incredible things and have accelerated the AI ecosystem. I hope that one outcome of this post is that agent framework builders can learn from the journeys of myself and others, and make frameworks even better. Especially for builders who want to move fast but need deep control. DISCLAIMER 2 : I'm not going to talk about MCP. I'm sure you can see where it fits in. DISCLAIMER 3 : I'm using mostly typescript, for reasons but all this stuff works in python or any other language you prefer. Anyways back to the thing...

title: GCWing/OpenBitFun
abstract:
English · 中文 Built to keep going. OpenBitFun is a highly customizable, open-source agent workspace that keeps work moving your way. Four powerful Agent Harness modes · Cross-device remote control · Customization from Mini Apps to source If this is the kind of agent workspace you want, ⭐ Star OpenBitFun and help more people discover it. Download Desktop · Mobile Releases · Mini App Marketplace · Join the community · Contribute demo.mp4 Four modes for the way you work The Agent Harness shapes how a task gets done. It plans steps, manages context, calls tools, coordinates agents, and brings their results together. Choose the mode that fits the task: Mode When to use it Minimal Quick collaboration. Start with a clear goal. The agent acts directly, you give feedback, and you refine the work together. Standard Everyday tasks. For work with several steps: plan the approach, work through it, and check the results. Ultimate Complex tasks. Dig into demanding problems, divide the work among agents, and bring their results together. Creative Creation and customization. Build Mini Apps or extend OpenBitFun's interface and capabilities to make the workspace your own. Switch computers. Control from your phone. Switch the device, switch the entire workspace. Choose another connected computer in the desktop app, and the interface switches to that device's sessions, workspaces, files, and task status. Move between your home computer, office computer, and server from the same app. Your phone is a remote controller. Send instructions, check progress, and respond to approval requests from your phone or browser. Tasks run on the selected host and keep going when you switch views or disconnect the controller. The official Relay is ready to use; no server deployment is required. Sign in on your devices with the same OpenBitFun account, using GitHub or an email verification code where supported. Same-network connections are also available. See the connection FAQ for login, internet access, and self-hosting requirements. On mobile, switch between layouts for one, two, or three screens. Focus on the conversation with a single screen, then unfold your phone to view conversations and files side by side. The interface adapts as the screen layout changes. Connection and deployment details Use SSH to work on a remote host, through a jump host, or inside a container. File access, terminals, and workspace commands target that environment; the Agent Runtime stays on the OpenBitFun host. The desktop app and CLI share core execution capabilities; mobile clients and messaging bots offer more ways to control tasks. Same-account device control uses the official Relay by default. Desktop can also run a local Relay for same-network mobile control. Both paths use the online OpenBitFun identity service for sign-in; LAN mode is not an offline-login option. A private Relay requires a matching client build: see the deployment guide . Device-to-device payloads are encrypted end to end with keys generated on the devices. Sessions and files are read from the owning online device on demand; the Relay still handles account, device, and routing metadata. This does not cover traffic to model providers, messaging bots, or published Pages. See the privacy boundaries , Remote Connect , and remote workspaces . Turn everyday needs into useful apps Build a Git insights panel for a repository, a workspace for presentations, or a form that brings routine actions together. Mini Apps turn specific needs into tools you can use. Describe what you need and let the agent build it. Each Mini App pairs a dedicated interface with an agent conversation, so you can use the app for everyday work and keep improving it through chat. Install and reuse the apps you build, or explore the Mini App Marketplace for tools that fit your work. Extend OpenBitFun with OpenBitFun Customize the roles, tools, interface, and source code. Start with an agent that fits your work, then extend the workspace around it: Build a specialist agent. Choose a model, define its role, and equip it with the tools and workflows it needs for motion comic production, visual design, code review, or your own field. Connect tools and workflows. Connect tools through MCP, turn repeatable processes into Skills, and use Hooks to customize how tasks run. Change the interface and source. Install skins for a new look, or modify the UI, tools, and runtime source to build your own version of OpenBitFun. You can ask OpenBitFun's Code Agent to modify and extend OpenBitFun itself. Learn more about agent management , Hooks and compatibility , and the product architecture . Built for sustained work The Rust Agent Runtime manages session state, context, and tool execution. Persistent sessions, interruption recovery, long-term memory, and support for extended tasks help keep work moving. Context compression and cache reuse help control resource consumption over longer runs. In this DeepSWE v1.1 evaluation, OpenBitFun achieved: GLM-5.3-Flash : 64.6% pass rate, 42.9 minutes median runtime (P50). DeepSeek-V4-Flash : 56.6% pass rate, 19.6 minutes median runtime (P50). More to explore These are just some of OpenBitFun's features. Explore more tools, workflows, and extensions as you put it to work on your own tasks. Where we're headed OpenBitFun is still evolving. Here are three directions we want to explore: Lights-Out Factory : Plan and design during the day, let tasks continue on a server, and come back the next morning to review the results. Infinite Radius : Extend from desktops and phones to wearables and embedded devices, so work can continue in more places. App Evolution : Enable more people to shape software, from personal tools to versions tailored to a profession or industry. Getting there means making long-running tasks more reliable, the runtime more efficient, and the desktop experience smoother. Build with it. Help shape it. Share what you build, offer feedback, or contribute code to help shape OpenBitFun. Share your use cases and experience, contribute agents, Skills, Mini Apps, or skins, or help improve the docs, interface, and runtime. Ideas and questions are welcome in this repository's Issues and Discussions. See the contribution guide for the development workflow. Download, setup, and running from source Get the Windows, macOS, or Linux package from the official download page . Install it, configure a model, and open a workspace to get started. See the user guide for usage instructions and download verification for package signature checks. Migration note: OpenBitFun 1.0.0 is not data-compatible with legacy 0.2.x releases. To migrate legacy data,
use the OpenBitFun Data Tools , currently available
for stable releases 0.2.17–0.2.19. To run from source, install Node.js 22.12+, pnpm 10.15.0, the Rust toolchain , and the Tauri prerequisites . Clone the repository, then run: pnpm install
pnpm run desktop:dev Desktop development supports frontend hot reload and automatic Rust rebuilds. See the CLI guide for the command-line workflow. Core code is licensed under the MIT License . Third-party dependencies and assets retain their own licenses. Thanks to the open-source authors and contributors who make this work possible. To report a vulnerability, see the security policy . Join the community Scan the QR code with WeChat to add us and request to join the OpenBitFun community group. Star History

It covers what most edits need: auto-captions, text-to-speech, background removal, keyframe animation, effects and titles, multi-track cutting, 4K export. With none of the catches: no watermark, no account, no subscription, no upload. Everything runs locally on a native Rust engine with a GPU compositor. Install it, drop in footage, cut. The AI models for captions, voices and cutout download once from Settings and work offline after that. Your footage never leaves your disk. Good for: TikTok, Reels and Shorts, YouTube videos, tutorials and screen recordings, podcast clips, memes. Also for machines: a built-in MCP server for AI agents ( concat --mcp , set up ) and a JSON-RPC API for scripts, so they can cut video with it too. Highlights 🚫 No watermarks. No account. No paywall. Ever. 🔒 100% local. Nothing uploads. Works offline. 💬 Auto-captions. Local Whisper. Pick a model size, get styled captions on the timeline. 🗣️ Text-to-speech + voice cloning. A free local voice on the desktop, or any voice from a few seconds of a recording. Phones are getting their own system voice. 🧍 Background removal. People, objects, or paint the mask yourself. 🎞️ Keyframes. Position, scale, rotation, opacity, volume, effect parameters. Curve editor built in. ✨ 100 effects, filters and transitions. GPU-rendered, live in the preview. ✂️ Cut fast. Split, trim, ripple, merge, freeze frame, speed. Magnetic timeline if you want it. 🎚️ Multi-track, multi-timeline. Overlays and picture-in-picture: stack video, stills and titles on as many tracks as you like. Several cuts in one project. Blend modes (screen, add, multiply…), crop, flips. 📝 Titles. Fonts, stroke, shadow, background plate. Presets to start from. 🎙️ One-switch voice cleanup. Denoise, enhance voice, level the loudness. Plus chipmunk, robot, telephone and friends. 📤 Export. H.264, HEVC, AV1. Up to 4K 60, 10-bit colour. 🦀 Native Rust engine. GPU compositor, proxies, hardware decode. 4K scrubs smoothly. 🤖 Scriptable. An MCP server built in, so Claude and other AI agents can edit with it ( one line to set up ), and a JSON-RPC API for scripts. A build from source adds gRPC and a command-line tool. 🖥️ macOS, Windows, Linux, Android. 26 languages. Same app, same project files. Download Two ways in: The website hands you the right build for your machine. Start here. GitHub Releases has every build for every platform, with installers, packages and checksums. For when you want to pick. Concat is in beta : it works, and it still has edges. Say so when you find one. Platforms ✅ Windows · x86_64 (ARM builds are paused, see #326 ). A setup and an .msi . If SmartScreen stops an unsigned build: More info › Run anyway ✅ macOS · Intel and Apple silicon. If macOS refuses to open an unsigned build: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Concat.app ✅ Linux · x86_64 and ARM. .deb , .rpm , .AppImage and an Arch package. Also a Flatpak on Flatpark , a community Flatpak remote that wraps the x86_64 .deb of each release and updates with it ✅ Android · phones and tablets ✅ iOS / iPadOS · iPhone and iPad, sideloaded ✅ Supported · 🚧 Work in progress · 🧪 To be tested System requirements and the optional model sizes are on the website . Code signing policy : why the Windows builds are not signed yet, and what Concat sends over the network (nothing you did not ask for). Build from source You need Rust 1.93 or newer (see rust-version in src/Cargo.toml ), the FFmpeg 7+ development libraries, cmake and a C++ compiler. macOS: brew install ffmpeg Windows: from FFmpeg's Windows downloads , take BtbN's win64-gpl-shared build (the one CI uses), unpack it and point FFMPEG_DIR at it Linux: use your distro's FFmpeg if it is version 7 or newer, otherwise use a BtbN shared build with FFMPEG_DIR like on Windows Then: cd src
cargo run -p concat # the editor window Other useful commands: cargo build --profile app -p concat # the shipping binary (fat LTO, stripped) cargo test # run the test suite cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings # what CI checks If you change text the interface shows, run python3 scripts/locales.py from the repo root so the string inventory stays in sync. Full details live in CONTRIBUTING.md . How to Contribute Important The best way to contribute is to grab a build from the Releases page and use it: find where it breaks, and say where it could be better. Ready to write code? CONTRIBUTING.md covers setup, the layout of the tree, the checks to run, and how contributions are licensed. Driving Concat from a script, a service or an agent? The developer docs cover the Concat API and its transports: JSON-RPC and gRPC; docs/MCP.md connects an AI agent over MCP. This Discussion is where the project was announced. title: Drones built to look like birds evaded detection at Air Force tech exercise
abstract:
A wing-flapping drone appearing to fly like a bird evaded sensor detection at a recent Air Force tech exercise in the Mojave Desert. Ornadyne’s small O1 ornithopter drone doesn’t use propellers like most drones. Instead, it mimics the flight mechanics of a bird by flapping its wings to stay in the air. The small unmanned aerial system (UAS) is designed to resemble a bird, while it collects intelligence or surveys an area at low altitudes. “It looks like a bird, it moves similar to a bird, and humans and counter-UAS systems can misclassify it as a bird,” Armen Arakelyan, one of Ornadyne’s co-founders, said in a Department of Defense release . “It’s also a lot quieter because we replaced propellers with flapping wings.” The test was part of the military’s annual “Game of Drones” event in September at Edwards Air Force Base, which sits in the Mojave Desert in Southern California. The base hosts drone exercises each quarter to test new tech. The event is sponsored by the Air Force 412th Test Wing’s Experimental Test Force and the Defense Contract Management Agency’s Blue List team , which approves commercial drones for sale to the U.S. military. It was the first time that the U.S.-based drone manufacturer tested its ability to hide from detection systems built by other private companies, said Arakelyan, who is also a former engineer for Elon Musk’s SpaceX. Mimicking a crow in shape and profile, Ornadyne’s O1 returns after a successful flight demonstration during “Game of Drones” 26-3 at Edwards Air Force Base, Sept. 17, 2026. Air Force photo by James West. The O1 drone weighs 1 pound and can fly up to 10 kilometers, which is a little more than 6 miles, for over an hour, according to a company fact sheet. The drone can carry a small payload, like a camera used to do target recognition for surveillance missions. Many drones are built to evade detection by masking the signatures they emit, using different frequencies or mobile SIMs , flying autonomously with a pre-planned flight path, or using fiber optic cables to bypass electronic surveillance. The O1 takes the method of blending in with the environment since the company says it can change the drone’s color, wingspan, proportions and silhouette to match a native bird species operating in a particular region. “We learned during ‘Game of Drones’ that sensors deployed by the other companies here could not establish our drone using their detection equipment,” Geourg Kivijian, Ornadyne’s other co-founder, said. “It registered as a bird, which is exactly what we wanted.” News Special operations guardians must ‘maneuver with their SOF counterparts,’ commander says By Patty Nieberg News An A-10 named ‘Rainbow Warrior’ sports Marilyn Monroe door art in the Middle East By Nicholas Slayton News Drones built to look like birds evaded detection at Air Force tech exercise By Patty Nieberg Add Task & Purpose (opens Google in a new window or tab) More information Adding us as a Preferred Source in Google by using this link indicates that you would like to see more of our content in Google News results. Ornadyne is not the first company to dream up a bird-like drone. The innovation also hasn’t been lost on a group of conspiracy theorists promoting, somewhat satirically, that Birds Aren’t Real . The notion behind the group’s claims is that the U.S. government has replaced all birds with surveillance drones . Well, they might not be far off. In fact, an entire category of unmanned systems known as ornithopter drones use ‘wings’ instead of propellers or jets to mimic birds or insects in the sky. In 2024, video of a People’s Liberation Army exercise showed a Chinese Jiaolong Commando — which are akin to the Navy SEALs — releasing their own bird-like drone resembling a Eurasian tree sparrow flapping its wings. Fortunately, the robo-birds in that video appear to be non-migratory.

title: Why I will not be using LLMs in my coding
abstract:
Why I will not be using LLMs in my coding Kristian Polso • November 8, 2026 AI programming This is a continuation to the past two blog posts I have made about coding and AI . After quite a lot of soul-searching, I have come to the conclusion that I will actively not be using any LLMs or AI agents in my professional work. It's been quite a rollercoaster this year, to say the least. There have been excellent articles and opinion pieces that have resonated with me and my feelings around AI usage. In this blog post I will list my biggest dealbreakers on why I won't be using LLMs in my work. Recommended reading I highly encourage everyone to read the essay 'Why I Resist Generative "AI"' from Esther Weidauer . They managed to articulate so much better than I ever could what's bugging me about the current enthusiasm of using AI in coding. Mind you, I do not 100% agree with every point in the article, but I definitely share the main sentiment and concerns. I especially like the section about how people argue that "LLMs are just a tool", but really, it is not, it is a SERVICE, where you outsource your work to the whims of a (usually US-based) third-party company. I know Machine Learning, trust me Before anyone calls me a luddite or a AI-skeptic, I want you to understand that I know Machine Learning. I have built production-grade ML implementations for several clients in my career for the past 10 years or so, like CNN-based image recognition models in Keras, air quality prediction models in Tensorflow and more. I have also dabbled with locally running LLMs and image diffusion models in my homelab, and have even contributed back in Github. LLMs and transformers are a cool and exciting technology, but the current hype and craze for them is frankly overblown and hazardous to people's work and health. My dealbreakers These are the dealbreakers, for me personally, on why I actively try not using LLMs in any of my professional work. Cognitive impact I've heard of the "LLM brainfog" from my fellow programmers all this year. And it's no wonder, there have been several studies confirming this: Self-Reported Reductions in Cognitive Effort and Confidence Effects From a Survey of Knowledge Workers (from MICROSOFT!) Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task Large-Language Models as a Cognitive Virus , how LLMs make you more and more reliant on using them for all tasks When I personally have used LLMs for several hours, I often feel disoriented and confused, and I feel like this is not a healthy thing for me to participate in. The quality of the output is not that great I feel that LLMs and their overtly verbose output trick less knowledgeable programmers of the quality of their output . When Claude spits out refactored code with tons of comments, documenting each method and variable, and tests for everything as well, it looks impressive, at a first glance. But if you dig deeper, it's sometimes just complete bullshit. I have had several cases at my day job where I've had to review Claude-generated code for bugs that could have been solved more elegantly with just a couple of lines of dense schema changes and migrations, but Claude had decided to build something completely new, utilizing the latest hooks and methods in the framework, outputting several tests for a single field etc. LLMs expose the literacy gap between great and mediocre coders . If you can't see how bad the generated code is, LLMs will only make you not see it faster. Maintainability is a nightmare Closely related to quality of code output, I've begun to see that the maintainability issue of LLM generated code is starting to creep in. If all of the code is written by agents, then at some point no human will understand what's going on, and that's not something I am comfortable with. Congratulations, you have let OpenAI/Anthropic/Elon Musk dictate what your code does and why. I like writing code I have written about this several times in the past. I just simply love writing code. It's part of my process of problem-solving. I constantly have small epiphanies when I write code; what's the optimal way to iterate over the content, where should this data be stored in the hierarchy of the application etc. This also applies to reading other people's code. I want to understand how the human behind the code thinks, plans and executes. What's their motivation, their goal, their field of expertise. AI has zero of this nuance in its output. Environmental aspect I probably don't need to say too much about this. Everyone has heard the news about new AI datacenters and their electricity usage ( sometimes even using new fossil fuel sources! ). Here in Finland, the news were briefly dominated by Google, on how they cut down hundreds of hectares of forest, without a permit, to build a datacenter . The "datacenter mania" is clouding people's minds and that's bad for the planet. Politics This is the hardest point for me to articulate. But I just personally feel squeamish about having my work being done by rather skeezy companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, or, god forbid, Cursor/SpaceX. Also, all the big AI providers are US-based, so there is definitely GDPR aspect to everything as well, me being an EU citizen. Everyone seems to have forgotten all about this in their big AI craze of 2026. Even though if a company SAYS the data stays in the EU region, remember that if they are a company based in the United States, CLOUD Act grants federal law enforcement authority to receive data stored anywhere in the world . There's been some talk online how "AI-assisted coding is tool of the elite", to lock you into a dependency of a commercial software in your line of work and livelihood. I feel it's been a bit exaggerated, but I can't help but feel like there's a nugget of truth somewhere in there. There's also positives, yes Now, there definitely have been positive moments when I have used AI tools in my coding work. For example, if I'm completely stuck somewhere in implementation, I can articulate a simple question to an AI agent and get somewhat of a coherent plan of execution forward. But in the end, the help I get from it I feel like is just not worth it, due to all of the above-mentioned reasons. AI is not inevitable I love how Esther Weidauer summarizes this argument: "AI is here to stay." OK. So is heroin. And I wouldn’t recommend that to anyone either. I keep hearing from all around me how inevitable AI is. And I would like to push back a little on this. Yes, AI-assisted coding is not going away. No technology can just disappear overnight. BUT it does not mean that you have to use it. With these subsidized token prices currently, I bet were seeing less and less AI usage encouragement in companies in the future. Even if some technology or tool sticks around, it does not necessarily mean its good idea to work with it. Conclusion This is probably my last post on this topic, at least for a while. I'm quite done researching and hearing about AI agents, harnesses and whatever else. I'm going back (or did I ever leave?) to old school coding. I tried writing this in a way where I share my personal feelings about this issue. I do not want to force or change anyone's opinion on AI-assisted coding. If you are happy with your current AI-assisted setup, then go for it. But these are my personal pain points that I have regarding its usage in the software world. Maybe I'm wrong, maybe I'm right, who knows. Frankly, at this point, I do not care, I just want to write my code in peace, with my human hands.

By default, all 6 routed experts per layer ( Top-6 ) are evaluated without pruning. title: GitHub New pull request overview page in public preview
abstract:
Back to changelog On a long pull request, checking what’s blocking often means scrolling past dozens of comments and timeline events just to reach the merge box. And once you’re there, you still need to work out what to do next. As people need to review more and more pull requests, time spent scrolling adds up. So we’ve begun to rethink the entire experience, beginning with addressing a familiar challenge: finding what’s blocking progress and determining what to do next. Today, we’re introducing the Overview page as an opt-in public preview, with rollout continuing through the weekend. It brings merge status and next available actions to the top of the page in a compact readiness summary. It’s the first step toward making pull requests easier to follow as code, conversations, and reviews evolve. The merge box, distilled We’re starting with the merge box, the place developers go to see whether a pull request can move forward. Rather than just moving it higher, we’ve also redesigned it to show the same information in less than half the space. Explore the supporting signals: A compact view of checks, comments, and approvals keeps the context nearby without making every detail compete for attention. Address what’s blocking: Take action to move the pull request forward, such as updating your branch. See if it’s ready to merge: Check merge readiness and merge when requirements are met. title: Show HN: Coldframe, a honeypot that poses as a supermarket fridge controller
abstract: I built Coldframe, a honeypot that pretends to be a supermarket refrigeration controller. Inspired by the events on industrial fridge installations in the past weeks, I wanted to see what people would try against a convincing fake. To learn more about this I built a honeypot that resembled perfectly the Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Dixell XWEB interfaces. Both of them are recognized on Shodan as real ones (an not as honeypots). It’s one Python file using only the standard library, and it builds on eppser/danfoss-ak-sm-decoy and public research by Synacktiv, Claroty and Ironhackers. Things that were fun to get right: - Matching real units. I used Shodan records of real devices to match header order, page titles, certificate fields and TLS versions. The Danfoss persona sends nginx headers in the same order as a real AK-SM 800A. The Dixell persona sends no Server header and pads its page to exactly 8,202 bytes. - Recognising exploit attempts. It recognises CVE-2025-41450, the Danfoss “code of the day” login bypass, and records whether the submitted code is correct for today. It also tags attempts targeting three other Danfoss CVEs and the XWEB vulnerabilities. - Letting them in. Default logins open a fake store dashboard with defrost buttons, so you see the second move, not just the first. Nothing behind it is real. Two instances have been live for a day. So far they’ve only seen generic scanners and Shodan’s crawler, which is called refrigerator.census.shodan.io. Feedback welcome, especially from anyone who has seen these devices in the field!

title: Agent memory needs its OpenTelemetry moment
abstract:
All posts Count the memory formats on your machine List every place your coding tools keep something they "remember". A typical setup today: an AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md in most repos, and .cursor/rules/*.mdc in a few an agent writing files to a /memories directory through Anthropic's memory tool Copilot keeping facts about each repo on GitHub's side a memory MCP server keeping a JSONL knowledge graph That's four different shapes, and none of them can read the others . A lesson your CI agent learns stays in whatever wrote it. Your editor agent can't read it, and neither can the next tool you try. Each format is reasonable on its own. Together, they rebuild the same small idea again and again: a note an agent left for its future self, stored at some address, true for a while. And the list keeps growing. Browse r/ClaudeAI, r/LocalLLaMA or r/cursor and you'll find a steady stream of "I built a memory layer for my agent" posts, each with its own storage, its own schema and its own MCP tools. That's good evidence the problem is real: people keep hitting it badly enough to build something. But every new solution adds one more format that nothing else can read. The problem isn't a missing tool. It's a missing agreement , and that only comes from the community working on it together. I build one of these tools, LoreKit, which is open source. This isn't a pitch that LoreKit has solved memory. Its format is one proposal among several, with gaps of its own. The point is that this is the moment to agree on a shared shape , and that another field has already shown how. We've seen this before Before 2019, every observability vendor shipped its own agent, its own instrumentation library and its own data format. Switching vendors meant instrumenting your code again. Two open projects, OpenTracing and OpenCensus, tried to fix that and competed with each other too. In 2019 they merged into OpenTelemetry . What mattered was what the vendors agreed to stop competing on: A data model : what a span, a metric and a log record are. Semantic conventions : shared names like service.name and http.* . A protocol : OTLP, one way to send the data. Reference implementations : shared SDKs and the Collector. Vendors kept competing on what they do with the data: storage, querying, analysis. Users instrument once. I work with OpenTelemetry every day at Dash0 , and that agreement is why a whole ecosystem of tools can read each other's data. The same four layers. Observability agreed on them and competes on what happens after the data arrives. Agent memory has plenty of implementations, but nothing agreed underneath them. Agent memory is where observability was before 2019. The timing is good: the formats are young enough to change, and there's already a neutral home for agent standards. MCP and AGENTS.md both sit under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation. A tour of the shapes These change quickly, so treat the details as a snapshot from late 2026. Family Example The unit of memory Addressed by Forgetting Instruction files AGENTS.md , CLAUDE.md , Cursor .mdc rules A whole Markdown file File path (plus globs for Cursor) Never. A person edits it Agent-managed files Anthropic's memory tool A file under /memories A path the model picks Never, unless the model deletes it Hosted repo facts GitHub Copilot Memory A fact with code citations One repository Deleted after 28 days unused Context blocks Letta core memory A labeled block with a character limit A label on an agent Never. Always in context Extracted facts Mem0 A fact the service extracts from messages user_id / agent_id / run_id / app_id Optional expiration date Namespaced store LangGraph BaseStore A JSON value dict A namespace tuple + key Optional TTL, reset when the item is read (by default) Knowledge graph MCP reference memory server Entities, relations, observations Entity name Never Temporal graph Graphiti / Zep A fact on a graph edge Entities + edge Facts are invalidated rather than deleted, on two timelines Addressed record LoreKit A record with a scope, key and lifecycle A scope string + key Never, unless a TTL is set A few of them got something right that a shared spec should keep. Copilot Memory pairs citations you can check against the code with forgetting by default, though it's locked inside one product. LangGraph shows how small the core can be: put(namespace, key, value) . Graphiti models time properly, with separate timelines for when a fact was true and when it was recorded. And AGENTS.md shows that a plain file at a known path can become a standard. The proposals that already exist Several people have started on this. MacPaw Research's Portable Memory is a .mem bundle with byte-reproducible serialization, deletion tombstones and optional signing; its authors say it isn't widely adopted yet. The Open Memory Protocol is an April 2026 draft for moving conversations and the memories derived from them between platforms as a ZIP with a manifest. Cognee's COGX format imports from Mem0, Letta and Zep. These mostly solve export : moving one person's memory from vendor A to vendor B. Coding tools also have a second, open problem: live addressing . When a CI job, an editor agent and a review bot work in the same repo at once, how do they read and write the same place and agree on what it means? A complete spec needs both. Export moves one owner's memory between vendors. Live addressing lets many tools share one place at the same time. The existing proposals focus on the first. A shared address could sit inside their records to cover the second. What a shared spec could look like Strip away the branding and every format answers the same four questions differently: where a memory is true, what its identity is (does a second write update it or duplicate it?), what it says , and when it stops being true . Nobody disagrees that those matter. The tools only disagree on the answers, which is where OpenTelemetry started too. There's one real fork: who writes the memory . In instruction files it's a person. In the memory tool, Letta and LoreKit, it's the model. In Mem0 and Graphiti, a service extracts facts from the conversation. A spec doesn't need to pick one. It needs to record which, so a reader knows how much to trust what it reads. Here's roughly what one record could look like as a file. It illustrates the data model; the field names aren't a proposal: --- spec : agent-memory/0.1 id : 8f0c2a6e-4b1d-4c7a-9e2f-3a5b6c7d8e9f address : { level : repo , value : github.com/acme/checkout } key : tests-need-local-postgres kind : lesson written_by : { type : agent , name : claude-code } content_type : text/markdown lifecycle : { expires_at : null , extended_by : write } attributes : { vcs.pr : 482 , ci.run_url : "https://ci.example/runs/123" } --- Integration tests fail with `ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432` unless Postgres is already running. Start it before `pnpm test` : docker compose up -d db The test setup does not start it for you. The frontmatter is the envelope: address and key say where it's true, id is its identity, lifecycle says when it stops, and written_by answers the fork. The Markdown below it is the memory itself, and content_type tells a reader how to treat it. Anything else a tool needs goes in attributes , under a namespace other tools can ignore. The same record serialises to JSON just as well, for a tool that wants to send it over the wire. Around that record, a spec would mirror OpenTelemetry's layers: Conventions : shared names for address levels ( global , project , repo , branch , and whatever monorepos need), for kinds, and for attribute namespaces ( vcs.* , ci.* , agent.* ), in one versioned registry. A contract : a few operations (write, read, list, search, archive) with fixed inputs and outputs, exposed over MCP. Many memory servers now offer an MCP interface, but each exposes different tools with different meanings.

title: Goodbye Claude, hello Pi
abstract:
I’ve been a longtime Claude Code user, ever since it became available in the Claude Pro subscription plan over a year ago. I remember the first time I used it, feeling giddy as it spat out messy Python code for whatever random weekend project I was working on, all from a single prompt. I’m certain that in a few years we’ll all look back at its release as one of the major drivers of this new era of software development we’re in. Despite this, due to an accumulation of many small frustrations, I’ve finally decided to retire it as my main coding harness and migrate my development setup to use Pi instead. Someone at Anthropic must’ve caught wind… just a day after making my decision, they announced Claude Code would finally start supporting AGENTS.md files in an effort to get me to stay. Unfortunately, for me it was too little, too late. In lieu of a proper obituary, I’d like to take this time to say a few words about the things I liked least about Claude Code (and thus what I’m looking forward to avoiding with Pi). The AGENTS.md thing kind of epitomizes the whole reason I decided to quit using Claude Code. Don’t get me wrong, having a ton of CLAUDE.md files scattered about various GitHub hobby repos is great guerrilla marketing. But it sucks for users to have to deal with copying or symlinking between the two formats. Like the Luddite I am, I still prefer to review most of the code it churns out before I commit it. I use(d) Claude Code inside VSCode, and it lets you connect the harness to the IDE. This is nice because you can highlight text in a file and have it automatically included in the context when asking questions or requesting changes during a review. Except you can only have one session “connected” to the IDE at a time. If you open a second tab to start another task while the first one works, it can’t receive the text selection events from the IDE at all. This has been reported at least as far back as December 2025 … and closed as a duplicate of a totally unrelated bug. 1 Of course, you can always use the official Claude Code VSCode GUI extension, which does allow you to have multiple tabs open and load the text selection into the context of each. But this extension has plenty of problems of its own. Half of the built-in slash commands don’t work at all in the GUI. It doesn’t have any support for a custom status line. Subagent output messages are simply layered into the main chat thread in chronological order, which is a mess to read when more than one is running. I could go on and on. In spite of all of these existing issues, it seems like Anthropic has worked at a feverish pace to pack more features into Claude Code without much care for quality or stability. Dynamic workflows , agent teams , ultrareviews – all great ways to help enterprise customers burn ever more tokens each day, but not really anything I want or need. Alongside all of these feature releases, they always seem to be fiddling with things in ways that mess up my personal setup. At the time of writing, there have been 244 releases to Claude Code this year; over 3/4 of these changed the system prompt or tool descriptions, which can substantially change how the LLM performs (especially when these new instructions contradict user prompts or repo conventions). And what are all those changes for? Despite chopping 80% of the system prompt , Claude Code still has way more overhead than Pi for seemingly no benefit. The default Bash tool’s description is almost 3,000 tokens, most of which is random stuff about using git and opening PRs on GitHub. 2 The models already know how to do this without detailed instructions, by the way. 3 This post has been a lot of hating. I’m sorry! That’s not my usual style, and I do think Anthropic has made a really cool piece of software here. I’m also not under any delusion that I would’ve done a better job if I were the one in charge of running Claude Code from the beginning. LLM coding harnesses are a very new space and being one of the first to innovate in a field is a really hard task. Later tools like Pi have the benefit of hindsight to see what works and what doesn’t, what’s a core feature and what can be cut. Ultimately, CC feels like a product without a strong vision or direction. It’s as if a bunch of excited engineers and PMs are rapidly tacking on whatever features suit their workflow… but without consideration for how this might make things worse for other users. It seems like there isn’t someone high-up whose job is strictly to say “no” to these requests, which is incredibly important when it comes to product engineering. So, for now, I’m leaving. I’m excited to lean more into Pi. The first few days required some finagling, but since then it’s been smooth sailing. I’m enjoying the stability, minimalist approach, and the extreme level of customizability. I’ve already written a couple of extensions to support my use cases, which I’m hoping to share soon after I’ve cleaned them up a bit. If you’re also feeling these frustrations, I’d highly encourage giving an open source harness a try! It’s not like there’s some huge technical roadblock to this either. After installing Pi, I wrote an extension to handle this very functionality across multiple open tabs in like 20 minutes. (return) Bonus points for the fact that it instructs the model to use cat <<'EOF' which (prior to widespread rollout of auto mode) would always trip the manual review rules regardless of existing git command allowlists. (return) If you assume 1 million DAU and 100M requests per day, trimming 1,000 tokens off of this could literally save millions of dollars in inference costs per year. Surely that’s worth some engineer’s time?? (return) I love hearing people's thoughts, so please don't hesitate to shoot me an email at calebdotsoftware@gmail.com . title: Risks of omission and commission errors when using generative AI in behavioral science research.
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly being adopted across the behavioral sciences, reshaping how researchers generate ideas, design studies, collect data, and analyze results. While GenAI offers substantial benefits such as increasing productivity, enabling more sophisticated methods, and lowering technical barriers, these gains come with potential costs in the form of errors. This article discusses the risks of errors as a foundation to decide when and how to use GenAI in behavioral research. We distinguish between two types of errors of shifting relative threat, depending on how narrowly a research task is specified. Open-ended tasks (e.g., ideation, literature review) leave a large space of plausible outputs and make researchers relatively more liable to errors of omission. In constrained, well-specified tasks (e.g., running a specified analysis, writing code to a stated scheme), the narrow solution space limits the scope for omission, raising the relative threat of errors of commission. We argue that commission errors are potentially easier to detect. Omission errors, by contrast, are harder to detect and pose greater risks to the diversity and scope of scientific inquiry. We propose that GenAI usage should be guided by a comparative assessment of error detectability. We offer practical recommendations for evaluating GenAI applications and for preserving the methodological diversity that sustains cumulative science.
